name: assert_fact
description: Assert a clinical fact into Lisa's working memory. Each fact has a type (e.g. gram, morphology) and a value. The bridge automatically files each fact under the correct context in the patient -> culture -> organism tree; you only name an organism (via 'entity') when a case involves more than one. Use this to build up the clinical picture before running inference.

fact_type.description: The type of clinical fact to assert.

value.description: The value for this fact. Valid values depend on fact_type. Organism-level morphology/staining: gram=(pos|neg), morphology=(rod|coccus), aerobicity=(aerobic|anaerobic), growth-conformation=(clumps|chains). Enterobacteriaceae species discriminators: lactose=(fermenter|non-fermenter), indole=(positive|negative), motility=(motile|non-motile|swarming), urease=(positive|negative), pigment=(red|none). Gram-positive coccus discriminators: catalase=(positive|negative), coagulase=(positive|negative), hemolysis=(alpha|beta|gamma), optochin=(sensitive|resistant), bacitracin=(sensitive|resistant), novobiocin=(sensitive|resistant), bile-esculin=(positive|negative), salt-tolerance=(tolerant|intolerant), arabinose=(fermenter|non-fermenter), sorbitol=(fermenter|non-fermenter). Culture-level: culture-site=(blood), culture-age=(integer as string). Patient-level: burn=(serious), compromised-host=(t), hospital-acquired=(t), recent-travel=(tropical), white-blood-count=(low), infection-site=(respiratory|abdominal|urinary), neutropenia=(t), prosthetic-material=(t), iv-drug-use=(t), age-group=(neonate|infant|adult|elderly). INERT VALUES -- accepted by this endpoint but matched by no rule in the current corpus: pigment=none, hemolysis=gamma, salt-tolerance=intolerant, age-group=(infant|adult|elderly), white-blood-count=low, and culture-age at every value. Assert them when the clinician reports them, so the record stays faithful -- but never SOLICIT one as a discriminating test, and never narrate its result as having moved the differential, because it did not. This list is a convenience copy of what `describe_rules` computes in `summary.parameters`; that is the authoritative version.

entity.description: Optional organism identifier (e.g. 'organism-1', 'organism-2'), used ONLY for organism-level facts (gram, morphology, aerobicity, growth-conformation, and every biochemical/disc discriminator: lactose, indole, motility, urease, pigment, catalase, coagulase, hemolysis, optochin, bacitracin, novobiocin, bile-esculin, salt-tolerance, arabinose, sorbitol) when a case has more than one organism, to keep each organism's evidence separate. Omit for single-organism cases (defaults to 'organism-1'). Ignored for patient-level facts (burn, compromised-host, hospital-acquired, recent-travel, infection-site, white-blood-count, neutropenia, prosthetic-material, iv-drug-use, age-group) and culture-level facts (culture-site, culture-age), which the bridge scopes automatically.

confidence.description: Confidence in this fact, from 0.0 to 1.0. Omit for full confidence (1.0). Use when the clinical evidence is uncertain (e.g. 'probably gram-positive' → 0.8).

name: run_inference
description: Trigger Lisa's forward-chaining inference engine. This fires all applicable rules against the current working memory and produces diagnostic conclusions with belief factors. Call this after asserting all available clinical facts.

name: get_conclusions
description: Retrieve the differential from the last inference run. Every rule states an ANSWER -- the SET of organisms its evidence narrows the question to -- and this endpoint combines them by intersection and reports what survives. Returns, per organism the corpus has NAMED in this consultation, an interval {bel, pl}: bel is belief committed to that organism specifically, pl is everything still consistent with it. It also returns `set_valued` -- belief committed to a SET without naming a member, 'one of this family, the evidence does not say which', which is often the honest headline; `conflict` (K), how much belief was committed to combinations that cannot all be true, WHICH MUST BE READ WITH `margin` AND NEVER ALONE -- two answers naming different organisms conflict totally here, so K counts how much rival evidence was OVERRULED and rises as the winning side strengthens; `margin`, how far the `leading_answer` sits above `margin_against`, the nearest answer that contradicts it, which is what says whether the conflict resolved (high K with a wide margin means rival evidence lost, not that the answer is shaky; high K with a margin near 0 is a genuine tie); and `hypotheses`, every organism any answer mentioned. A rival can be a SET whose members each have bel 0, so `margin_against` may name something `hypotheses` does not rank. NOTHING IS EVER EXCLUDED BY BEING NAMED: an organism loses plausibility because other answers narrowed away from it, not because a rule argued against it. An organism NO rule mentioned is not listed and is not thereby excluded -- its plausibility is the residual ignorance, the honest statement that nothing has spoken to it, and the corpus does not model every organism that exists.

name: get_rule_trace
description: Retrieve the rule trace from the last inference run. Shows which rules fired and in what order, providing an audit trail for the diagnostic reasoning. Use this to explain the reasoning behind conclusions.

name: explain_conclusion
description: Retrieve the AUTHORITATIVE, engine-recorded account of why an organism stands where it does. Returns the `argument`: every answer given about this culture, each with the set it `narrows_to`, its belief, the `rules` that said it (with verified `provenance` -- origin, literature `evidence`, `belief_basis`, and a clinical note), and an `admits` flag saying whether that answer still leaves this organism standing. ANSWERS THAT DO NOT ADMIT IT ARE RETURNED TOO, and they are the point: nothing in this corpus argues against anything, so an organism loses plausibility only because other evidence named something else. Also returns `intersection` (what the admitting answers leave when combined), `bel`/`pl`, `conflict`, and a plain-language `narrative` you may quote. NOTHING CHAINS: there is no nested derivation and no arithmetic composing one belief through another. Never reconstruct this reasoning or recall a citation from memory -- call this and narrate what it returns.

organism.description: The organism to explain, exactly as it appears in get_conclusions (e.g. 'klebsiella'). An organism no rule has named returns 404 -- its plausibility is simply the residual ignorance.

name: describe_rules
description: Retrieve the AUTHORITATIVE catalogue of the diagnostic rulebase, read from the compiled rules themselves. Every rule is CONFIRMING: it states the ANSWER its evidence narrows the question to -- a SET of organisms -- with a positive belief. There are no ruling-out rules, no negative strengths, and no organism-class: a genus IS a set, so 'is this a staphylococcus' is a question about {aureus, epidermidis, saprophyticus} rather than about a separate fact. Per matching rule: its `narrows_to` (the organisms its evidence leaves standing), its `resolution` (how many that is -- 1 is a species call, more is an honest 'one of these'), its `belief`, the `premises` it requires with the values they must take, and its `provenance` (origin, verified literature `evidence`, `belief_basis`, and a clinical `note` giving the rule's basis and why it is weighted as it is). MORE EVIDENCE GIVES A SMALLER ANSWER: urease positive answers 'one of four', urease positive with swarming answers 'Proteus', and the second sits inside the first so they agree rather than compete. You do NOT hold the rulebase in memory: call this before stating any rule's answer, premises or citation, and whenever the clinician asks what the system knows or which test would best discriminate. The `summary` gives the corpus shape: how many rules, which organisms they can speak about at all, the `parameters` it can act on, and the distribution of `resolutions`. An organism absent from `summary.organisms` is one the corpus cannot name -- say so plainly rather than reasoning about it. `summary.parameters` is the corpus's INPUT vocabulary -- every observation some rule actually reads, with the values it can take -- and it is the authoritative answer to 'which test should we run next?'. A parameter or value absent from it is INERT: the bridge will accept the assertion and return success, no rule will match it, and the differential will not move. NEVER recommend a test whose result this corpus cannot act on; a clinician who orders it gets an answer that can never be entered. Check here before naming any test you have not already seen in a rule's `premises`.

names.description: An organism (e.g. 'klebsiella'). Returns every rule whose answer ADMITS it -- what would have to be true for this organism to be identified, and which coarser answers still leave it standing. This is the query for 'why might this be Klebsiella?' and for 'which test next?'.

premises.description: A finding, named EITHER by its parameter ('urease', 'lactose', 'motility') OR by the value it took ('neg', 'non-motile', 'positive'). Returns every rule that reads it -- what this finding buys you. Prefer the PARAMETER form when asking what a test is worth, since it returns the rules for every value that parameter can take, both polarities included; the value form narrows to one reading. An empty result means no rule reads it at all, which is a real answer -- but check the parameter form before reporting a finding as uninformative, because a value that no rule reads may still have a sibling reading that several do.

name.description: An exact rule name (e.g. 'burn-blood-aerobic-gram-neg-rod-narrows-to-opportunist-rods'), for when a trace, partial match, or explanation has already named a rule and you need its detail.

name: get_partial_matches
description: Check which rules have some but not all conditions satisfied by current working memory. Returns rules that are 'close to firing' — showing which conditions are already met and which facts are still needed. Use this to determine what questions to ask the clinician next.

name: reset_session
description: Clear all facts from working memory and reset the session. Optionally switch the active belief system as part of the reset. Use this when starting a new patient case or when the clinician wants to start over.

belief_system.description: Optional: switch the active belief system on this reset. 'cf' = certainty factors (Shortliffe-Buchanan); 'ds' = simplified Dempster-Shafer. Omit to keep the current setting.

name: recommend_therapy
description: Ask the deterministic therapy solver for an antimicrobial regimen covering the organisms currently identified in working memory. Call this ONLY after inference has produced organism conclusions (run get_conclusions first). The solver — not you — chooses the drugs: it computes a minimum set cover, picking the fewest drugs covering every organism whose identification belief clears the coverage threshold, applies patient contraindications, and reports anything it cannot cover. Its objective is drug COUNT only — it has no notion of spectrum, so 'fewest' is not 'narrowest' and must not be narrated as stewardship. The response also carries 'alternative_agents' (other drugs that covered but were not chosen) and 'alternative_regimens' (other equally minimal regimens the tiebreak chose against), which is where questions about narrower options are answered from. It carries 'set_obligations': the SET-valued answers the regimen had to cover ('one of these seven, the evidence does not say which'), each with its 'mass' and any 'uncovered' members. A set is a coverage REQUIREMENT, not a differential entry -- no member is claimed as the organism, so never narrate it as treating a particular species; narrate the group. A non-empty 'uncovered' there names an organism the evidence says could be the infection and the regimen does not treat, which is a real gap and must be stated. It also explains blocked narrowing: a narrower agent may cover every named organism yet miss a set member, which is why culture-1 stays on meropenem even under spectrum-sparing. It carries 'below_threshold' too: the organisms the gate DROPPED, each with 'covered_by' -- the chosen regimen's drugs that cover it anyway, with susceptibility. CHECK 'covered_by' BEFORE SAYING AN ORGANISM IS UNTREATED: a regimen entry's 'covers' lists only the organisms the solver was targeting, so a runner-up the regimen happens to cover looks absent from it, and reporting it as untreated is false. An empty 'covered_by' is the real gap and should be stated plainly. The gate's own value is echoed as 'coverage_threshold' (with 'susceptibility_threshold'); quote it from there and never from memory -- it has been retuned before. You NEVER pick, add, or substitute a drug; your job is only to relay the patient's contraindications and narrate what the solver returns, citing coverage, doses, exclusions, and — when asked — what it passed over. NOT FOR CLINICAL USE — the pharmacology knowledge base is schematic and illustrative.

patient.description: Patient-state tokens that trigger drug contraindications. Include every one the clinician has stated (e.g. a penicillin allergy → 'allergy-penicillin'; pregnancy → 'pregnancy'). Omit or pass an empty array when there are no contraindications. Only listed tokens are honored; anything else is ignored by the solver.

solver.description: Which solver to use. Defaults to 'exact', which enumerates every minimum-size regimen and so can also report the ones it chose against. 'greedy' is the original approximation, kept selectable for comparison; it returns the same-size regimen but no alternative_regimens. Omit unless the clinician explicitly asks for a different solver.

gate.description: Coverage-gate policy for belief-valued (interval) susceptibilities — a stewardship dial. 'belief' (default) is conservative: an agent covers only if the LOWER bound of its susceptibility interval clears the threshold. 'plausibility' is optimistic: it covers unless there is evidence against (uses the upper bound). 'midpoint' splits the difference. Omit for the conservative default; pass a different value only if the clinician wants to explore how the regimen changes under optimistic vs conservative stewardship. The response echoes the gate used.

objective.description: Which objective breaks ties among equally minimal regimens. Drug COUNT is primary either way; this only chooses the tiebreak. 'lexicographic' (default) maximizes susceptibility × identification belief — today's behavior, which tends to pick the broadest agent because breadth and susceptibility correlate. 'spectrum-sparing' minimizes declared spectrum breadth first, implementing narrow-spectrum preference. Pass 'spectrum-sparing' only when the clinician asks about narrowing or de-escalation, and NEVER present its result as simply better: it buys narrowness with a lower coverage floor, and because breadth is blind to WHO AWaRe reserve status it can escalate a reserved agent (e.g. enterococcus moves from ampicillin, an Access drug, to linezolid, a Reserve drug). Narrate the trade in both directions. The response echoes the objective used.
